stops.name: Worms on the Rhine, the birth of Johanna Eckert
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the city (NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division finding aid, Hanya Holm Papers; en.wikipedia, 'Hanya Holm'). A minority secondary entry gives 1888 instead and is not followed. The birth house is not located in any source reached and the pin is the cathedral quarter. The father's trade is in open conflict: de.wikipedia calls Valentin Eckert a Gastwirt, an innkeeper, while an American encyclopedia entry, unreachable this session, is cited for wine merchant. The mother's maiden name is spelled Moerschell in German sources and Moerschel in English ones.
stops.campa: Johanna Josepha Eckert is born at Worms on the Rhine, under the towers of the imperial cathedral, to Valentin Eckert and Marie, born Moerschell. German sources call the father an innkeeper; an American reference calls him a wine merchant, and nobody has reconciled the two. Of the mother it is said that she experimented and held patents, though no reachable record shows one. Nobody in the household has ever been on a stage, and nothing in it points toward dancing. The Grand Duchy of Hesse is twenty-two years inside the German Empire, and the house the child is born in has not been located.

stops.campa: Twenty miles downriver the Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary keeps a girls' school that the Germans call the Convent of the English Ladies. The Eckert daughter is sent there and taught by nuns. She credited the convent later with forming her, and the discipline is legible in every account of how she ran a studio sixty years afterward; what the girl made of it at the time nobody wrote down. Latin, needlework, music, the daily offices, an order of hours that does not vary from one week to the next.

stops.campa: She goes to Frankfurt to study piano at Dr. Hoch's Conservatory, an instrument that asks a person to sit still for hours at a time. The story her interviewers repeat afterward is that a teacher told her she was not the sitting type and needed movement rather than a keyboard. Whether anyone said it or not, she leaves the piano. She can read a score, though, which separates her from most dancers of her generation, and she never afterward treats music as accompaniment. She is twenty-one when she enrolls, and no source reached says how long she stayed.

stops.name: Hellerau, the Dalcroze certificate
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (NYPL finding aid: graduated from the Dalcroze Institute at Hellerau, 1916); the month is a placement. Substantive caution carried into the campa: Jaques-Dalcroze himself left Hellerau in 1914, was barred from Germany, and opened his Geneva institute that year, so a 1916 certification on that campus belongs to the successor school rather than to his own Bildungsanstalt. Pin inherited byte-identical from jaques_dalcroze.journey.json, stop 'Hellerau, the Bildungsanstalt opens its doors'. A separate dossier claim of a Dalcroze Institute of Applied Rhythm at Frankfurt rests on one bare Wikipedia phrase, contradicts de.wikipedia's account, and carries an invented coordinate; it is not made a stop here.
stops.campa: In the model garden city above Dresden she takes her certificate in eurhythmics, the method Emile Jaques-Dalcroze built so that a musician would feel a measure in the body before naming it with the mouth. He is not there. The war took the school's money and a protest signature took his residence permit; the Bildungsanstalt has passed to successors who teach his doctrine in rooms he designed. Holm arrives in the second generation, and what she holds when she leaves is a qualification in another man's system, issued by people who learned it from him. It is 1916 and the war has two years to run.

stops.campa: She marries a painter, Reinhold Martin Kuntze. She is twenty-four, certified in a method rather than trained in an art, and teaching rhythm to other people's children in a country that is losing a war it has not yet admitted it is losing. The record of the marriage is thin to the point of transparency: one secondary encyclopedia entry, a year, a name, no parish, no witnesses, no photograph reached. Everything else known about it is known from its ending. No civil register was located, and the place is a guess.

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, five years of teaching the method
stops.date_confidence: attested for the activity and the span (NYPL finding aid: taught the Dalcroze method and music from 1916 through 1921). The schools, towns and employers of those five years are not itemized in any source reached; the Frankfurt pin is her best-documented base in the period rather than an attested workplace, and the 1918 date is a placement inside the span.
stops.campa: For five years she teaches rhythm and music in the Dalcroze way: clap the measure, walk the phrase, let the arm carry a beat the foot is not carrying. It is respectable work and it is not dancing. Germany between the armistice and the inflation is full of such classes, bodies being reformed by method, and thousands of women pass through them and remain teachers of them for life. She is one of the thousands for five years. Which schools, which towns, which employers, no source reached itemizes.

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the divorce and the son
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout. The February 1921 divorce and the existence of a son, Klaus, come from secondary encyclopedia summaries and an NYPL summary respectively; no civil record of either was located, and Klaus's birth date and birthplace are established by nothing reached. He is independently attested only at the far end of the story, as the person she is buried beside. The pin is Frankfurt for want of any recorded place.
stops.campa: The marriage ends in February. There is a son, Klaus. Where he was born, who kept him, what was agreed between the parents, none of it is written in anything reachable; the accounts say only that when she sailed for New York ten years later the boy stayed in Germany with his father. Klaus Holm surfaces again seventy-one years on, at the other end of the story, as the grave she is lowered into beside. Between those two facts the record holds nothing: not a school, not an address. Whether mother and son saw one another at all in the years between is a question nothing reachable answers.

stops.name: Dresden, watching Mary Wigman dance
stops.date_confidence: attested that seeing Mary Wigman perform is what turned her from music toward movement (NYPL finding aid). The year is given as 1920 by some accounts and 1921 by others and is left unresolved here. No source reached names the hall or the programme; the pin is central Dresden and the November date is a placement.
stops.campa: She is twenty-seven or twenty-eight, a certified teacher of rhythm, and she goes to watch Mary Wigman dance. Wigman works to a gong and a drum, and sometimes to nothing at all, and treats the air around her as an adversary with weight in it. This is the reverse of everything Dalcroze taught: not a body obeying a score, but a body setting the terms. She has come to dance a decade later than anyone else in the room. Holm enrolls at the Wigman school within the year; whether that year is 1920 or 1921, the sources do not agree.

Holm's entire working life afterward is an argument for the second half of it.

She tours Europe with the group for five years and teaches the classes when it comes back. She is not the most arresting dancer on the stage, and everyone in the house, herself included, knows it. Her gift is for taking a doctrine that arrived in the world as one woman's seizure and making it teachable to a room of strangers. From 1924 the school's teaching is hers to run, and the street number of the rooms she ran it in was not recovered.

Palucca has gone to found her own school. Georgi and Kreutzberg are going out as soloists. Holm stays.

stops.campa: Two summers running she is brought to a Dutch country estate to make dances for the Star Camps, the mass gatherings the Order of the Star in the East holds on land given to it at Eerde. Thousands sleep under canvas in the park for the congress. It is her first work at that scale and the first time she directs rather than dances. Holm stages the movement: choruses in the open air, amateurs by the hundred, no proscenium, no lighting rig, a field and a slope.

How near this mass choreography stands to aesthetics the next decade put to other uses is a question scholars have not stopped arguing.

stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the renaming (en.wikipedia: Hanya Holm Studio from 1936, Hanya Holm Dance Company founded the same year; Dance Teacher magazine, 'Hanya Holm: German Expressionism'). The motive is disputed and left unresolved: political distance from Wigman's accommodation with the Third Reich, commercial necessity, or both. stops.campa: The Wigman name comes off the door. In Germany Mary Wigman is making her peace with the new state; in New York the word German has become a liability on a dance school's letterhead, and the anti-Nazi feeling of the people who pay the tuition is not an abstraction. The school becomes the Hanya Holm Studio and a company is founded under the same name. Whether she did it to stay solvent or to put distance between herself and her teacher, the sources disagree, and she never settled it in print.

Bennington's summer audience sees the work first, on the campus where the American field argues with itself in the open for six weeks a year. It is the largest thing anyone in modern dance has attempted here, and the woman who made it has been in the country six years. That the summer showing came before the New York premiere reconciles two sources; neither states it.

stops.date_confidence: unresolved between two sources and deliberately left so. Dance Teacher magazine says the troupe folded in 1944 after eight years for financial reasons; the NYPL finding aid, the stronger source and the one the rest of this file follows, says the company dissolved in 1947 after thirty original pieces and frames her concert-dance career as 1936 to 1947. The stop sits at 1947 on NYPL's authority; the 1944 figure is recorded, not discarded. Month and day default to the first of January.
stops.campa: The Hanya Holm Dance Company stops. One account puts it at 1944 after eight years, another at 1947 after thirty original works, and nobody has reconciled the two; both give the same reason, which is that she could not finance another season. Modern dance in America in the forties is a thing you subsidize out of tuition fees, and the fees are finite. She keeps the school and she keeps the summer school in Colorado. She does not form another company.

stops.name: Colorado College, the summer school founded
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the institution (NYPL finding aid; Colorado College Bulletin, Cossitt mural article). The June date is a placement at the head of a summer session; no opening date was recovered.
stops.campa: She founds a summer school of the dance at Colorado College, in a town under Pikes Peak with thin air and a long light. She will run it for forty-three consecutive summers, longer than the New York studio lasts and very much longer than the company. Students come from across the country for six weeks and go home teachers. What the mountains give her that Vermont could not is her own institution, on her own terms, with nobody else's technique in the next studio contradicting hers through the wall. The first session opens in the June of 1941.
sources: NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division finding aid, Hanya Holm Papers
Colorado College Bulletin, Cossitt mural article (sites.coloradocollege.edu)

stops.name: Colorado College, Alwin Nikolais at the summer sessions
stops.date_confidence: [R] for the date. Alwin Nikolais trained under Holm at Bennington, became her assistant at the New York school and taught with her at Colorado College in the summers (en.wikipedia, 'Alwin Nikolais'); no source reached dates the start of the Colorado assistantship, and 1948 is a placement inside the period. Nikolais has no journey file in the corpus. The quotation is carried at one remove: en.wikipedia gives it, attributing it to Walter Sorell, Hanya Holm: The Biography of an Artist (1969), pp. 102-103; the Sorell text itself was not reached, archive.org's copy being borrow-restricted and its search API returning 403.
stops.campa: Among the students who follow her out of Bennington is Alwin Nikolais, who becomes her assistant in New York and teaches beside her through the Colorado summers. Mary Wigman's Dresden reaches the second half of the American century through him more than through anything Holm choreographed. He takes the part of the teaching that is not steps: space as a material, improvisation as a discipline rather than a licence, the dancer as one element among light and sound rather than the subject of the piece. He builds a multimedia theatre out of it. When the Colorado assistantship began, nothing reached says.
stops.quote: You have a perfect right to branch out, if you have the stuff in you, if you discover your own richness, if you have something to say.
stops.quote_source: Hanya Holm, quoted in Walter Sorell, Hanya Holm: The Biography of an Artist (Wesleyan University Press, 1969), pp. 102-103; reached only via en.wikipedia, 'Hanya Holm'

stops.name: Central City Opera House, The Ballad of Baby Doe
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the venue and the credit (en.wikipedia, 'The Ballad of Baby Doe': premiere 7 July 1956 at Central City Opera, Colorado, directed by Hanya Holm and Edwin Levy; NYPL finding aid).
stops.campa: The Ballad of Baby Doe, an opera about a Colorado silver fortune and the woman who outlived it guarding a played-out mine, has its premiere in the mining town where the story happened, up a canyon west of Denver. Holm directs it with Edwin Levy. She is sixty-three and has been coming to this state every summer for fifteen years. My Fair Lady had opened in New York four months earlier: one season hands her the largest musical on Broadway and a new American opera in a mining town. The date is 7 July 1956.

stops.name: Colorado College, the honorary doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the award (NYPL finding aid: honorary Doctor of Fine Arts, Colorado College, 1960). The June date is a placement at commencement and is not documented.
stops.campa: Colorado College makes her a Doctor of Fine Arts. She holds no university degree of any kind; her credentials are a certificate from a Dalcroze school that no longer exists and a diploma from a Wigman institute in a country she left twenty-nine years ago. The college has had her for nineteen summers by now and is honoring a faculty member as much as a figure of the field. She accepts it in a state she first came to in 1936 to give a concert nobody in New York would review. In December of the same year Camelot opens on Broadway.
sources: NYPL Jerome Robbins Dance Division finding aid, Hanya Holm Papers

stops.name: New Century Theatre, Kiss Me, Kate
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the venue, the run and the credit (en.wikipedia, 'Kiss Me, Kate'). The pin is the theatre's own recorded coordinate at 205-207 West 58th Street and 926-932 Seventh Avenue, correcting a coordinate in the dossier that sat some 240 metres too far west; the house, formerly Jolson's 59th Street Theatre, was demolished in 1962 and 200 Central Park South stands on the site. stops.campa: Cole Porter's musical about a company staging The Taming of the Shrew opens two days before the new year and runs one thousand and seventy-seven performances. Holm's dances are not set-pieces dropped in between the songs: they belong to the characters and to the show inside the show, and they stop when the story needs them stopped. Producers notice. She is fifty-five, an Ausdruckstanz dancer out of Dresden by way of Vermont, and she has been in the country seventeen years.

stops.name: Washington, the choreography entered in the register
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the fact (NYPL finding aid). The scope matters and the narrower wording is used here: NYPL says the registration made her the first choreographer of a Broadway show ever to receive such protection, which is not the same as the broader claim, circulating in secondary sources, that this was the first choreography copyrighted in the United States. The Copyright Office is the institutional site of a filing and not a place Holm is recorded as visiting; no visit is claimed. Month and day default to the first of January.
stops.campa: The Kiss Me, Kate dances are written down in Labanotation, the movement script Rudolf Laban devised so that a dance could exist on paper the way a score does, and the notated document is registered for copyright. No choreographer of a Broadway show has held such protection before. The law did not change; the evidence did. Until a dance could be written down there was nothing to deposit and nothing to infringe. Holm is not recorded as having gone to Washington for any of it.

stops.name: New York, The Golden Apple
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, the work and the Critics' Circle citation (NYPL finding aid). No source reached this session names the New York theatre or the opening date; the March placement and the theatre-district pin are both provisional and should be replaced the moment a venue is confirmed.
stops.campa: The Golden Apple moves the Iliad and the Odyssey to Washington State at the turn of the century and sings the whole of it through, with no spoken dialogue to hide the transitions in. Holm's choreography takes a Critics' Circle citation. It is the sort of show that collects prizes and loses money. Which New York house it opened in, and on what night, is recorded in nothing reachable, which is an exact measure of how much of a choreographer's record survives. The year is 1954.

stops.name: Mark Hellinger Theatre, My Fair Lady
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the venue and the credit (en.wikipedia, 'My Fair Lady'), pinned to the theatre's own recorded coordinate at 237 West 51st Street, about 180 metres from the dossier's point. The Tony nomination for Best Choreography came at the eleventh Tony Awards in 1957, not in 1956 as the dossier's chronology lens had it; 1956 was the first year nominees were published at all, so no earlier Holm nomination can exist. Michael Kidd won that year for Li'l Abner.
stops.campa: My Fair Lady opens and does not close for six and a half years. Much of Holm's work in it is not what an audience would call dancing: the Ascot crowd moving with a slowness that reads as a species under observation, the servants, the street. Building movement out of character rather than out of steps is by now the thing producers hire her for. The Tony nomination arrives the following spring, at the first ceremony ever to publish its nominees, and Michael Kidd wins it for Li'l Abner.

stops.date_confidence: [R] for the venue. The 1959 Vancouver Festival staging of Orpheus and Eurydice is attributed to the NYPL finding aid via the dossier; that it played the Queen Elizabeth Theatre, which opened that year, is a plausible but unconfirmed match, and the July date is a placement inside a festival season.
stops.campa: She stages Orpheus and Eurydice for the Vancouver International Festival, her first work in Canada. The city has just opened a new theatre, the festival is two years old, and whether the production played that house is not recorded in anything reached. The opera is the one in which a singer is permitted to lead the dead back on the single condition that he not look behind him, and he looks. Holm is sixty-six and has been directing opera for three years.

stops.name: Toronto, the O'Keefe Centre restaging
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The NYPL finding aid is cited via the dossier for a restaging at the O'Keefe Centre, Toronto, the year after Vancouver. The venue opened in 1960, which is consistent, but the booking itself was not independently confirmed and the October date is a placement.
stops.campa: The Vancouver Orpheus is carried east and restaged at Toronto's O'Keefe Centre, a house opened that same year. That is very nearly the whole of the record: a city, a year, a building, one line in an archival summary. She is working now in three countries and two forms, opera direction and musical comedy, and the concert dance she came to America to teach has been behind her for thirteen years. Nothing of the Toronto production, its cast, its reception, its dates, was recovered.

stops.name: Majestic Theatre, Camelot
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the venue and the credit (en.wikipedia, 'Camelot'), pinned to the theatre's own recorded coordinate at 245 West 44th Street, about 170 metres west of the dossier's point. One dossier claim is dropped as false: Camelot ran 873 performances, fewer than Kiss Me, Kate's 1,077 and far fewer than My Fair Lady, so it did not outlast every other show she worked on.
stops.campa: Camelot opens at the Majestic, the second of the Lerner and Loewe shows she choreographs, and runs eight hundred and seventy-three performances. It is the shortest of her three great runs and the one whose songs travel furthest afterward. Nobody watching the knights dance can see that the movement came out of Dresden. What follows is teaching and the summers in Colorado, for thirty-two more years. She is sixty-seven, and Broadway will get no new musical out of her again.

stops.date_confidence: [R] for the site. stops.campa: She takes the head of dance at a musical theatre academy in New York, a fourth institution added to a working life that already holds a studio, a summer school and a Broadway career. She is sixty-eight years old. The shape of the rest of it is set here: no more companies, almost no premieres of her own, the whole of the work passing into other people through rooms, six-week sessions, and corrections called aloud across a floor. She has thirty-one years left and will spend most of them teaching.

stops.name: New York, the studio closes
stops.date_confidence: one-year discrepancy flagged, not resolved. The NYPL finding aid gives 1968 as the closing year and is followed here; en.wikipedia's '1936-1967' is a span of operation that the dossier's geography lens read too literally as a closing date, putting 1967 in one lens against 1968 in another. Pin inherited from mary_wigman.journey.json. Month and day default to the first of January.
stops.campa: The New York school closes after thirty-two years, or thirty-one, depending which source is doing the counting. What outlives it is paper: tuition ledgers, roll books, expense records, the names of everyone who ever paid to stand in those rooms. Thirty-seven years of New York in a box of receipts. The villa on Bautzner Strasse, where she learned all of it, is by now behind a border in a state calling itself the German Democratic Republic, and dance is still being taught in it. She is seventy-five, and she goes on teaching elsewhere.

stops.name: Juilliard, Lincoln Center: teaching at eighty-one
stops.date_confidence: [R]. en.wikipedia has her teaching at the Juilliard School from 1974 onward; no appointment record was reached and the September date is a placement at the head of an academic year. Martha Hill, who founded the Bennington School of the Dance in 1934, directed Juilliard's dance division in this period; that is attested independently of Holm's appointment.
stops.campa: At eighty-one she joins the faculty at Juilliard, where the dance division is run by Martha Hill, who forty years earlier put her on a Vermont lawn beside Martha Graham, Doris Humphrey and Charles Weidman and let the four of them contradict one another in front of the students. The two women have been in the same profession, and largely on the same side of it, since before either had a reputation to defend. Holm teaches. She will go on teaching for the better part of another decade.

stops.name: New York, Jocose for Don Redlich
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The NYPL finding aid, through a Don Redlich Papers cross-reference, gives 1982 for Jocose, made for Redlich's company when Holm was in her late eighties; the date could not be re-verified and no premiere venue was recovered, so the pin is New York City generally. Mikhail Baryshnikov's White Oak Dance Project later toured the work: that is White Oak's traveling and not Holm's, and it is recorded here as a source on her own stop rather than staged as a scene of its own. Month and day default to the first of January.
stops.campa: In her late eighties she makes a new dance, Jocose, for Don Redlich's company. Redlich came out of her studio, so the work goes to a former student the way nearly everything she made went to former students. It is the last choreography in the record under her name. Years afterward a company of celebrated dancers picks the piece up and tours it again, which is not an arrangement she made and not, so far as the record shows, a performance she ever sat and watched.

stops.name: Colorado College, the forty-third summer
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the count (Colorado College Bulletin, Cossitt mural article: the final season of a forty-three summer run begun in 1941). The July date is a placement inside the session.
stops.campa: She directs her last summer at Colorado College. Forty-three of them, 1941 to 1983, unbroken: she was forty-eight when it began and she is ninety when it ends. Nothing else in her working life ran anything like that long, not the New York school, not the company, not Broadway, not the ten years in the Wigman house at Dresden. It ran through a world war, through the whole of her Broadway career, and on through her seventies and her eighties. Six weeks a year in a mountain town, forty-three times over, and then it stops.

She is ninety-five. The same year a documentary about her is released, narrated by Julie Andrews and Alfred Drake, with Alwin Nikolais and Murray Louis interviewed in it. Some accounts date that film to 1984 instead, and nobody has settled which is right.

stops.name: New York, the death at ninety-nine
stops.date_confidence: attested (NYPL finding aid; en.wikipedia: died 3 November 1992 in New York City, aged 99, of pneumonia). A minority secondary entry gives 5 November, age 103, and a birth year of 1888; the institutional record, NYPL and the Internet Broadway Database, holds 3 March 1893 and 3 November 1992 and is followed. No hospital, address or borough is named in anything reached, so the pin is New York City generally.
stops.campa: She dies in New York of pneumonia, ninety-nine years old, sixty-one years after landing there on a German school's contract and expecting to go home. One reference gives the date as the fifth and the age as a hundred and three, working from an 1888 birth year the archives do not support; both versions put the death in the same week of the same November. She had outlived Mary Wigman by nineteen years and Martha Graham by one, and she had gone on teaching until nine years before the end.

stops.name: Hanover Township, Pennsylvania: the grave beside her son
stops.date_confidence: attested at township level (en.wikipedia, 'Hanya Holm', citing Reynolds and McCormick, No Fixed Points, Yale University Press, 2003: she and her son are interred in Hanover Township, Luzerne County, Pennsylvania). The cemetery name circulating in the dossier, Hanover Green, is unsupported by anything reached: Hanover Green is one of the township's villages, not a confirmed cemetery, and Find a Grave returned 403. The pin is the township centroid given by en.wikipedia, 41.20000 and -75.87444, adopted to replace two conflicting dossier coordinates that differed from each other by about three kilometres. The burial date is nowhere recorded; the date shown is a placement shortly after the death of 3 November.
stops.campa: She is buried in a township in the anthracite country of northeastern Pennsylvania, beside Klaus, the son left behind in Germany in 1931. Not Worms, not Dresden, not New York, not Colorado Springs. No source reached explains the choice, and the likeliest explanation is also the plainest, which is that it is where her son already was. She had not lived with him since he was a boy in a country she left under contract, expecting to return within a season or two. Which cemetery in the township holds the two of them is established in no record found.
